knowledge_point.title: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating

question.:question/problem:
Find the nonconstant local solution to $y'=2(x - 3)\sqrt{1-y^2}$ by separating variables. Work on a local branch where the sine argument $\theta$ satisfies $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$. Express the solution as $y=\sin(\boxed{\text{expression}}+C)$.

Expression: {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x - 3)\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x - 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2(x - 3)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arcsin}⁡y & ={(x - 3)}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $y=y(x)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $y.$ This gives

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡({(x - 3)}^{2}+C)
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

This nonconstant branch applies where $-\pi/2<(x - 3)^2+C<\pi/2$, so $\cos((x - 3)^2+C)>0$. The constant endpoint solutions $y=\pm1$ also solve the ODE.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x - 3)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8{(x - 3)}^{3} & =5 \\ {(x - 3)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5+8{(x - 3)}^{3} \\ \text{d}y & =(5{(x - 3)}^{-2}+8(x - 3))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \text{d}y & =\int (5{(x - 3)}^{-2}+8(x - 3))\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-5{(x - 3)}^{-1}+4{(x - 3)}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(4)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4) & =6 \\ -5(1)^{-1}+4(1)^{2}+C & =6 \\ C-1 & =6 \\ C & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-5{(x - 3)}^{-1}+4{(x - 3)}^{2}+7 \\  & =-\frac{5}{(x - 3)}+4{(x - 3)}^{2}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x - 1)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x - 1)}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x - 1)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-{e}^{-(x - 1)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-(x - 1)}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-(x - 1)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(1)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{0}+C) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ C-1 & =\frac{1}{4} \\ C & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-(x - 1)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{4}-{e}^{-(x - 1)}).
$$

$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(-1)=11$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-1) & =11 \\ 6(1)^{1/2}+2(1)^{2}+C & =11 \\ C+8 & =11 \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =6{(x + 2)}^{1/2}+2{(x + 2)}^{2}+3 \\  & =6\sqrt{(x + 2)}+2{(x + 2)}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to $\sin(x - 4)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-\left(4 x - 16\right)\sin(x - 4)=\cos(x - 4)$ that satisfies $y(\frac{\pi}{2} + 4)=\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}$. Assume that $4<x<\pi + 4$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first rearrange and separate, then integrate and apply the initial condition.

$$
y'=\frac{\cos(x - 4)}{\sin(x - 4)}+4 x - 16.
$$

Use $v=\sin(x - 4)$, so $\mathrm{d}v=\cos(x - 4)\mathrm{d}x$. On the given interval, sine is positive. Thus

$$
\int\mathrm{d}y=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}+\int \left(4 x - 16\right)\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
y=\ln(\sin(x - 4))+2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2}+C.
$$

At $x=\frac{\pi}{2} + 4$, $\sin(x - 4)=1$ and hence

$$
\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}+C,\qquad C=0.
$$

Therefore $y=2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2} + \ln{\left(\sin{\left(x - 4 \right)} \right)}$.
